name: Jute Mallow
harvestProduct: fresh leaves and young shoots (mucilaginous when cooked)

evidence.quote: Jute mallow grows well in summer when temperature is above 27 °C and performs better in well drained sandy clay loam soils, but also grows in a wide range of soils.
evidence.doc: Production Guidelines for African Leafy Vegetables, WRC Report TT 536/12, 2012

frostTender.notes: No DAFF/DALRRD production guideline exists for jute mallow (confirmed absent via exhaustive Wayback CDX search of nda.agric.za, nda.gov.za and dalrrd.gov.za). The only South African primary source found (WRC/PGALV) describes it only as a warm-season crop (>27°C) and never uses the word 'frost' or states a minimum/cold-tolerance temperature for it. frostTender=true is a reasonable inference for a tropical Corchorus species but is NOT a directly sourced SA statement — flagged honestly as inferred, not quoted.

evidence.quote: Sowing and Transplanting: Mix seed 1:10 with sand or dry soil. Sow in rows or broadcast. Thin the seedlings out (1-2 cm apart) to ensure that you have stronger seedlings. Transplant seedlings when they are about 7-10 cm tall, as older plants will not grow well.
evidence.doc: Production Guidelines for African Leafy Vegetables, WRC Report TT 536/12, 2012

transplant.notes: Both direct sowing/broadcasting and transplanting (at 7-10cm seedling height) are described as options.

daysToHarvestRange.notes: GAP: no explicit days-to-first-harvest figure found in any South African source. The WRC/PGALV guideline describes management (seed dormancy of 4 months before sowing, transplanting at 7-10cm) but never states a sowing-to-first-pick day count. A non-South African source (Biovision Africa Trust / eoai-africa.org, a Kenyan smallholder growing guide) states 'ready for the first cutting in about 60-70 days' — recorded here only as unverified non-SA supplementary context, not used as the sourced SA value, per the sourcing rules for this catalog.

harvestPeriodWeeksOrMonths.value: Repeat cutting 3-4 times per planting; 2-week succession sowing recommended to spread the marketing period.

evidence.quote: Harvest Jute mallow by picking the tops or cut young growth back at about 15 cm above the ground level. New side shoots will develop and harvesting can be repeated 3 or 4 times.
evidence.doc: Production Guidelines for African Leafy Vegetables, WRC Report TT 536/12, 2012

evidence.quote: Plant Jute mallow at an interval of two weeks to spread the marketing period.
evidence.doc: Production Guidelines for African Leafy Vegetables, WRC Report TT 536/12, 2012

evidence.quote: Spacing for tall varieties is 10 cm in the row by 30-50 cm between rows. Broad varieties with many side shoots require a spacing of 30 x 50 cm.
evidence.doc: Production Guidelines for African Leafy Vegetables, WRC Report TT 536/12, 2012

rowSpacingRangeCm.notes: Figure is for 'tall varieties' specifically. For 'broad varieties with many side shoots' the source gives '30 x 50 cm' without stating which dimension is the row and which is in-row — recorded as ambiguous.

evidence.quote: Spacing for tall varieties is 10 cm in the row by 30-50 cm between rows. Broad varieties with many side shoots require a spacing of 30 x 50 cm.
evidence.doc: Production Guidelines for African Leafy Vegetables, WRC Report TT 536/12, 2012

inRowSpacingRangeCm.notes: 10cm applies to 'tall varieties'; the 30cm figure is the ambiguous dimension of the 30x50cm 'broad variety' spacing (see rowSpacingRangeCm notes) — not a second, distinct in-row measurement for the same variety type.

sowDepthRangeCm.notes: No sowing depth stated in the source.

yield.notes: GAP: no fresh-leaf yield figure (t/ha) found. No DAFF/DALRRD guideline exists for this crop; the WRC/PGALV guideline (the only SA primary source found) contains no quantitative yield data for any of its 8 covered crops. An ARC-VOPI nitrogen-response trial on Corchorus olitorius (Maseko et al., Acta Horticulturae 2019, ISHS) was located via its abstract but gives only qualitative yield statements, not exact t/ha figures, and the full paper could not be accessed (network-blocked). MDPI, ScienceDirect, ResearchGate and Tandfonline searches for a quantified SA yield trial were all blocked in this session.

ecocrop.row: Corchorus capsularis (proxy — the edible C. olitorius is not itself listed in ECOCROP; C. capsularis is the closest congener present, grown mainly for fibre, not as a leafy vegetable)

gaps: No DAFF/DALRRD production guideline exists for jute mallow (confirmed absent by exhaustive Wayback CDX search of nda.agric.za, nda.gov.za and dalrrd.gov.za for jute/Corchorus/delele terms).

sowMonths could not be sourced at all — the WRC/PGALV guideline (the only SA primary document covering this crop) has no month-by-month planting/harvest schedule, unlike the individual DAFF crop brochures.
daysToHarvestRange is unsourced for South Africa; only a non-SA (Kenyan) figure was found, and per the sourcing rules it is not used as the value.
No fresh-leaf yield (t/ha) figure found in any consulted source.
Sow depth and seed rate not stated in the source.

No South African cultivars or named varieties found; the source distinguishes only informal 'tall' vs 'broad' plant types, not named cultivars. No ARC-VOPI accession/line names for this species were located.
No South African production-zone information (which provinces grow it) was found in the WRC/PGALV guideline or elsewhere.

Family is given here as Malvaceae (the modern placement for Corchorus) since the source materials consulted do not state a family for this genus explicitly; older literature (e.g. the FAO/PROTA-type references cited elsewhere in this catalog) places Corchorus in Tiliaceae — noting this as it may cause inconsistency with older reference material.
summary: No DAFF/DALRRD guideline exists for jute mallow; the only South African primary source is the WRC/DAFF Production Guidelines for African Leafy Vegetables, which gives spacing, transplanting and repeat-harvest practice but has no sowing-month schedule and no yield figures for any crop it covers. Days-to-harvest and yield are unsourced gaps for South Africa; only a non-SA Kenyan smallholder guide provided a first-cutting figure (60-70 days), which is noted but not used as a sourced value.
